subject: probability-and-statistics
subtopics: the arithmetic mean of a data set, the weighted mean and the mean of a grouped frequency table, and the mean as the balance point
the median: position (n+1)/2 for odd n, the average of the two middle values for even n, and its robustness to outliers
the mode, ties and bimodality, and the mode as the only summary available for non-numeric data
how the mean, median and mode sit together in symmetric and skewed unimodal distributions, and the empirical relation mode = 3 median - 2 mean
the mean, median and mode of a grouped frequency table: class midpoints, the median class and the modal class with continuous boundaries
the variance and standard deviation of a data set, the divisor N against n - 1, and the shortcut form
what a shift and a scale do to the mean, the median, the mode, the variance and the standard deviation
signed deviations, the minimisation of squared deviations at the mean and of absolute deviations at the median, and why squaring is used
the median and the mode of a random variable: the two-condition definition, non-uniqueness, and the exponential and normal cases
the standard deviation of a count: the binomial sqrt(np(1-p)) and the Poisson sqrt(lambda)
the effect of one changed or added observation, the combined mean of two groups and the combined variance
choosing which summary to quote, the units of variance against standard deviation, and the coefficient of variation

chosen.title: Descriptive statistics formulas
covers: the arithmetic mean of raw and grouped data
the median of raw and grouped data, with the continuous-boundary warning
the mode of grouped data and the modal-class convention
the two-condition median of a random variable and the F(m) = 1/2 case
the minimisation of squared deviations at the mean and of absolute deviations at the median
population against sample variance and standard deviation
the effect of y = ax + b on the centre and the spread
the combined mean and the combined variance
chosen.why: The only GATE-oriented written source found this run whose full text could be read, and the only one that states both minimisation identities and the combined-variance between-group term. Every formula on it was checked by recomputation before a card used it, and one of its claims (the sample against population conversion) is the only place the relation s^2 = (n/(n-1))sigma^2 appears in this topic's sources.

chosen.title: Lec 4, Central Tendency and Dispersion - I
covers: the arithmetic mean and its sensitivity to extreme values
the weighted mean and a worked credit-weighted example
the mean of grouped data as a weighted mean of midpoints
the median position rule for odd and even counts and its robustness
the median and mode of grouped data
when to use the mean, the median or the mode, from the skew of the data
signed deviations summing to zero, the mean absolute deviation, and the two reasons for squaring
chosen.why: The only lecture this run whose transcript could be followed through the whole central-tendency sequence, and the source of the two-reasons-for-squaring statement and the signed-deviations identity that card 8 rests on. Chosen over the coaching channels because it teaches the reason for each formula rather than a shortcut, and over MIT OCW because it is a single readable lecture rather than a video page with no transcript body.

chosen.title: Lecture 04: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
covers: the mean on eleven retirement ages, and the outlier that moves it
the median on the same data and why it barely moves
the mode, and why it is the only summary for rating data
the empirical relation median - mode = 2(mean - median)
the standard deviation as the positive root of the mean squared deviation, worked on five dog heights
chosen.why: A second course and a second lecturer, deliberately, so the robustness and empirical-relation cards are not built on one voice. It is also the only readable source that shows the same data set analysed by all three summaries side by side, which is exactly the comparison the trap on card 4 turns on.

chosen.title: Introductory Statistics 2e, sections 2.6 and 2.7
covers: the symmetrical case where mean, median and mode coincide
the bimodal case where the modes differ from the mean
the direction the mean is pulled in each skew
the sample divisor n - 1 against the population divisor N
the standard deviation as a measure that is always positive or zero
chosen.why: A standard text independent of both lecture courses, used to corroborate the skew direction and the two divisors. It is the only source read this run that states the standard deviation is always positive or zero, which card 6 and card 12 both rely on.

chosen.title: Sankhyiki: NCERT class 11 mathematics chapter 13 notes and summary
covers: the ladder from central tendency to dispersion
the statement that a measure of centre alone hides the spread
variance as the mean of squared deviations and the standard deviation as its positive root
the step-deviation method and the grouped standard deviation
why the standard deviation is preferred to the mean deviation
chosen.why: The only readable non-English written source, and the one that supplies the argument for why dispersion is needed at all - two data sets with the same mean and different spreads. That argument is what card 12 and the opening of card 6 are built on. Everything taken from it is rendered in English and the cards that use it say so.

chosen.title: Mean, Median and Mode in Tamil - continuous (grouped) data
covers: the grouped mean as sum(f*m)/N on a five-class table
the median class and the interpolation formula
the modal class and the interpolation formula
chosen.why: The only Tamil source whose transcript could be read, and it earns its place by working one complete grouped table through all three formulas: classes 0-10 to 40-50 with frequencies 12, 18, 20, 25 and 23, giving a mean of 2740/98 = 27.96, a median of 29.5 and a mode of 37.14. All three numbers were recomputed here before use. It is the worked example on card 5's original question.

chosen.title: GATE Overflow for GATE CSE, Volume 1 - Engineering Mathematics: Probability (chapter 7)
covers: the question numbering of every GATE CSE probability question since 1987
the classification that separates CSE engineering-mathematics questions from General Aptitude and other-branch questions
chosen.why: The index that made the search for this topic's PYQs systematic instead of a guess: its chapter 7 lists two CSE questions under Statistics and shows that the mean, median, mode and standard deviation material in a CSE paper is thin, which is why four of the five PYQs here sit under other headings (Random Variable, Normal Distribution, Probability, Expectation). No question text was taken from it, because its text layer drops inline mathematics; the text came from the question pages.

chosen.title: Probability subject notes - the Statistics section
covers: mean, median and mode as measures of central tendency
variance and standard deviation as measures of dispersion
range as max minus min
the population against sample variance conventions
the binomial and Poisson standard deviations
chosen.why: The GATE-oriented framing: it is the only readable text this run that states each summary in the words a GATE answer key would use and lists the sample-against-population convention as a pitfall. Read in part through the search service's extract.

standard_refs: Sheldon Ross, A First Course in Probability, chapter 2 and chapter 4 (the mean as an expectation, and the median condition) - the book GATE preparation pages recommend for this subject
Ronald E. Walpole, Raymond H. Myers, Sharon L. Myers and Keying Ye, Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists, chapter 1 (measures of central tendency and variability) and chapter 8
NCERT Mathematics, Class 11, chapter 15 'Statistics' (mean, median, mode and the measures of dispersion for raw, discrete and continuous data) and the CBSE Applied Mathematics chapter 4
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, chapter 2, sections 2.6 and 2.7 (skewness and the mean, median and mode; measures of the spread of the data)

GATE 2027 CS syllabus, Engineering Mathematics line 'Random variables. Uniform, normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation. Conditional probability and Bayes theorem.'
notes: The syllabus names this topic in four words, so the twelve subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Walpole chapter 1, NCERT class 11 statistics, the OpenStax descriptive-statistics chapter and the IIT Roorkee lecture order), not a quotation from the syllabus. Each of the four words - mean, median, mode, standard deviation - gets at least two cards, and the grouped-table, deviation, invariance and count cases are included because they are where the four words are actually examined.

Five GATE CSE previous-year questions were verified for this topic: 2011 Q.33 (mean, median and mode invariant, standard deviation scaled), 2014 Set 2 Q.2 (an expected word length as the mean of nine lengths), 2017 Set 1 Q.19 (the median of max(X, 0)), 2021 Set 2 Q.22 (the standard deviation of a binomial count) and 2024 Set 2 Q.44 (the mean of a product is bounded by the mean). Four of the five sit under other headings in GATE Overflow's own index, which is the honest measure of how thin this topic's dedicated question record is.

Every PYQ is SOURCED against a GATE Overflow accepted answer, not key-verified against an official answer key: the official papers and keys were not fetched this run, so no marks field is recorded on any record and every question reference follows the paper numbering as reproduced by the sources, with the GATE Overflow numbering given where it differs.

No YouTube caption track was readable this run, so no card quotes or timestamps a video and videoRefs is empty on every card. The two lectures used were read through third-party transcript pages, and both are PARTIAL: the IIT Roorkee transcript through its weighted-average example, the Tamil lecture through its mode computation.

Two sources are non-English and both are marked translated: a Hindi summary of the NCERT class 11 statistics chapter and a Tamil lecture on grouped data. Everything published is English. No card quotes a Hindi or Tamil sentence; what is used is the structure, the formulas and one worked table, all recomputed here before publication.

The 2024 Set 2 Q.44 question sits on the boundary between this topic and the Random Variables topic, because it is a statement about means of random variables. It is recorded here once, on the mean card, and deliberately not duplicated there.

Five of the twelve cards carry no previous-year question of their own - the median, the mode, the grouped table, the deviation identities and the choice of summary - because no verified CSE question in this topic is decided by them alone. Each says so on the card rather than borrowing a question that does not test it.
